items.title: Jack DeJohnette — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: That had Benny Maupin on bass clarinet, tenor, voice and Dave Holland

ctx.x: Yeah. We did one more record, and actually there was an instrumental that I wrote called “Festival” that CBS wanted to push as a single, but again we had no money to go out and tour. So at that point I said “Okay I’m gonna go sink or swim with jazz.” They let us out of the contract, and I went back to deciding to be a bandleader and I think

my first band had John Abercrombie… I had been working with a group with John and Mick Goodrick; master guitarist and educator who teaches at Berklee. I had the two guitars and a bassist named Clint Houston. So I called on John. John had been working with Chico Hamilton, and so John played spacy guitar and could go a lot of places I wanted to go. (He) had a sense of humor. So, I think that first bass player was named Peter Warren at the time. I was looking for a saxophone player and I think that Alex Foster was…

items.title: Jack DeJohnette interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 7, 2025
items.q: and then he would play or somebody — Bennie Maupin would play, different players would solo on top of that.

ctx.x: And there’s a quote in here from you, “I got around so well on Miles’ music because I like the unexpected.” Was “Bitches Brew” an unexpected situation for you or had you been sort of set up for that?

Yeah I was set up and prepared. I’m from Chicago, where I played various kinds of music. So I didn’t have any biases toward all the so-called genres of music. You know “Bitches Brew” was basically kind of a jam session with — not highly arranged, but with, you know, melodic interludes in between things. And then Miles let the tapes roll and got a groove that he liked and then he would play or somebody — Bennie Maupin would play, different players would solo on top of that. And then through Teo Macero,
his producer, through his artistry of putting all the different tracks together to tell a story, he did that very well.
